paragraphs: Min-max optimization involves competing objectives: one side seeks to minimize a quantity while the other seeks to maximize it. This paper studies problems that also impose constraints and lack the usual convexity and concavity properties. Its guarantees apply to a structured class called comonotone problems, including a more general mathematical formulation called comonotone inclusion.

The first contribution extends Extra Anchored Gradient to this constrained setting. The authors establish a convergence rate of O(1/T), where T is the number of iterations, and show that this rate is optimal among first-order methods for the studied class. They also prove that the iterates themselves converge to a solution, a separate guarantee from a decreasing error measure.

The second contribution extends Fast Extra Gradient and establishes the same rate over what the abstract describes as the broadest comonotone inclusion class studied so far. Both analyses use potential functions to track progress. These arguments may also help analyze other accelerated algorithms, while the stated guarantees remain tied to the comonotone structure.
icml-2024-accelerated-algorithms-for-con.tldr: The paper extends two accelerated algorithms to constrained comonotone problems, proving optimal O(1/T) convergence rates.

paragraphs: A climate answer can sound clear and polished while still falling short as a communication of scientific knowledge. This paper builds an evaluation framework that treats those qualities separately. Drawing on science communication research, it examines both how an answer is presented and whether it is adequate in its treatment of knowledge.

The framework evaluates responses across eight dimensions and thirty issues, allowing a more detailed assessment than a single overall judgment. The researchers apply it to several recent language models using diverse climate questions. This design makes the evaluation about the quality of climate communication, including aspects that surface fluency alone cannot capture.

The paper also introduces an oversight protocol combining AI assistance with raters who have relevant education, with the aim of making evaluation scalable. The results identify a substantial gap between surface qualities and epistemological qualities. That finding means strong presentation should not be taken as sufficient evidence of strong climate information, and it supports evaluating these aspects explicitly rather than collapsing them into one impression.
icml-2024-assessing-large-language-model.tldr: A science-informed evaluation finds a substantial gap between how well LLM climate answers are presented and their epistemological quality.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a target probability distribution with a distribution that is easier to work with. Many black-box implementations optimize an evidence lower bound, or ELBO. The paper identifies noisy gradient estimates and sensitivity to hyperparameters as reasons these methods can converge slowly, and proposes batch and match, abbreviated BaM, as an alternative.

BaM optimizes a divergence based on scores, which describe how log probability changes with the variables. For Gaussian approximations with full covariance matrices, the method admits a closed-form proximal update. This gives a direct update rule for a family that can represent correlations, rather than relying on the usual stochastic ELBO optimization procedure.

The theoretical result concerns a Gaussian target and the limit of infinite batch size: under those conditions, the estimated mean and covariance converge exponentially quickly. Experiments also cover non-Gaussian targets from hierarchical and deep generative models. In these tests, BaM typically needs fewer gradient evaluations than leading ELBO-based implementations, sometimes substantially fewer. The experiments therefore extend the evidence beyond the setting of the convergence proof.
icml-2024-batch-and-match-black-box-vari.tldr: BaM uses score-based matching and closed-form Gaussian updates to reduce gradient evaluations in tested variational inference problems.

paragraphs: A language-conditioned agent must connect a textual request to behavior in an environment. One approach scores rendered images with a vision-language model and uses those scores as reinforcement learning rewards. Training a separate policy for every task is costly, while multi-task training requires a suitable task collection and can generalize unreliably.

This paper separates interpreting the request from executing it. First, it searches for an environment configuration whose rendered appearance receives a high score for the task description. Then a pretrained goal-conditioned policy moves the agent toward that configuration. The language model supplies a target, while the policy supplies the ability to reach it.

The authors also explore distilled models and scoring configurations from multiple viewpoints. Multiple views address ambiguities that arise when a configuration is judged through just one two-dimensional image. In the Humanoid environment, the resulting agents outperform multi-task reinforcement learning baselines on zero-shot generalization. Their training requires neither textual task descriptions nor other environment-specific annotations, demonstrating this separation of language interpretation and control in the tested setting.
icml-2024-bridging-environments-and-lang.tldr: The method turns language requests into visually scored target configurations that a pretrained goal-conditioned policy can reach.

paragraphs: CodeIt approaches the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, or ARC, as programming from examples: the model must produce a program that maps given inputs to the desired outputs. A major obstacle is sparse reward. Sampled programs rarely achieve the requested result, leaving little successful experience from which the model can learn.

The method alternates between generating programs and learning from stored experience. After a sampled program runs, hindsight relabeling changes its recorded goal to the output it actually produced. This turns an unsuccessful attempt at the original goal into an example of a transformation the program did accomplish. Prioritized replay then determines which experiences receive attention during learning.

Combined with pretraining and data augmentation, this process supports generalization across ARC tasks. The paper reports solving 15% of evaluation tasks, outperforming existing neural and symbolic baselines and achieving state-of-the-art performance in its evaluation. It also describes CodeIt as the first neuro-symbolic approach to scale to the full ARC evaluation dataset. The contribution is a way to extract useful training signals from otherwise unrewarded program samples.
icml-2024-codeit-self-improving-language.tldr: CodeIt learns from what sampled programs actually accomplish, using prioritized hindsight replay to solve 15% of ARC evaluation tasks.

paragraphs: Models pretrained on abundant text or images can be difficult to adapt to specialized data such as protein sequences or cosmic rays. The target data may differ substantially from the original modality, while labeled examples are scarce. PaRe addresses both problems by generating intermediate forms of data during cross-modal fine-tuning.

A gating mechanism selects important patches from source and target examples. A patch replacement procedure then preserves and combines these patches to create intermediate modalities arranged from easier to harder. This gives the model a gradual transition between data types, while also providing enriched training material beyond the limited target examples.

The approach is trained end to end and uses a modality-agnostic replacement scheme. The paper reports improved stability and transferability through this gradual bridging process. Across three benchmarks covering more than ten modalities, PaRe outperforms the compared hand-designed, general-purpose, task-specific, and state-of-the-art cross-modal fine-tuning approaches. These results support intermediate data generation as a practical way to help pretrained models adapt when both modality differences and limited target data make direct transfer difficult.
icml-2024-enhancing-cross-modal-fine-tun.tldr: PaRe gradually mixes selected source and target patches to improve model transfer across modalities with limited labeled data.

paragraphs: An average treatment effect summarizes an intervention with one number, but researchers may also want to understand how it changes the distribution of outcomes. This paper develops a regression adjustment method for estimating such distributional effects in randomized experiments. Its goal is to improve precision by using information measured before treatment.

The method incorporates these pre-treatment covariates into distributional regression and allows standard machine learning tools to estimate the supporting components. Those components help adjust the treatment-effect estimator. The validity claim is conditional: the nuisance components must be estimated reasonably well. The approach therefore combines flexible prediction with a statistical requirement on the quality of those estimates.

The authors establish large-sample properties and a uniformly valid inference method, supporting uncertainty assessment as well as point estimation. Simulations and a real-data analysis show reduced estimator variance in finite samples. The stated practical benefit is more precise distributional treatment-effect estimation from randomized data, extending attention beyond mean effects while making use of readily available machine learning methods.
icml-2024-estimating-distributional-trea.tldr: Machine learning regression adjustment improves precision for distributional treatment effects, with validity depending on adequate nuisance estimation.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph prediction requires attention to how nodes work together and how they are connected. The paper argues that existing Shapley-based approaches can miss part of this picture by assigning only individual node importance or perturbing inputs without respecting graph structure. It introduces the Myerson-Taylor interaction index to incorporate structure into both node and interaction attributions.

The index breaks groups of nodes into components according to a chosen connectivity criterion. This makes the graph's organization part of the attribution rule itself. The authors prove that the index uniquely satisfies five specified axioms addressing graph structure and higher-order interactions. That uniqueness is relative to the stated axiom system.

The resulting explainer, MAGE, uses the second-order version of the index to identify important graph motifs. It looks for structures that push a prediction positively as well as negatively, making explanations sensitive to opposing contributions. Across the tested graph datasets and models, MAGE consistently produces better subgraph explanations than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The empirical contribution connects the formal interaction rule to identifying influential structures in model predictions.
icml-2024-explaining-graph-neural-networ.tldr: MAGE explains graph predictions using a structure-aware interaction index that identifies motifs with positive and negative influence.

paragraphs: Deploying a language model under different compute and memory budgets can otherwise require training multiple versions. Flextron offers an architecture and post-training optimization framework that turns an existing trained model into a flexible collection of nested subnetworks. The aim is to support different deployment requirements within one model.

Its elastic structure can adapt at inference time to user-specified latency and accuracy targets without additional fine-tuning. Flextron also adapts to the input, using routing algorithms to direct tokens through its subnetworks. These two mechanisms address different needs: selecting an operating configuration for deployment and choosing computation based on the tokens being processed.

The paper introduces a sample-efficient training procedure for this transformation and evaluates it on GPT-3 and Llama-2 model families. It reports better performance than multiple separately trained variants and other elastic networks. The reported training run uses 7.63% as many tokens as original pretraining. These findings support reusing a trained model across resource requirements with substantially less training data than the original pretraining run consumed.
icml-2024-flextron-many-in-one-flexible-.tldr: Flextron converts a trained LLM into nested, token-adaptive subnetworks that support different inference budgets without further fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Generative models often need to produce related information in both discrete and continuous forms. Protein co-design is one such problem, because it jointly generates a sequence and a structure. This paper introduces Discrete Flow Models, or DFMs, to make discrete data compatible with a multimodal flow-based generation framework.

The central idea uses continuous-time Markov chains as the discrete counterpart of flow matching in continuous spaces. Although the states are discrete, transitions are modeled over continuous time. The resulting formulation includes discrete diffusion models as a special case, while allowing approaches that improve on existing diffusion-based methods.

The authors combine DFMs with continuous modeling in a shared multimodal framework and apply it to protein co-design. They report state-of-the-art performance for joint sequence and structure generation. The same multimodal model also supports flexible generation of either sequence or structure. The contribution therefore includes both a discrete generative formulation and a demonstration that it can connect different data types within one model, rather than requiring a separate modeling framework for each.
icml-2024-generative-flows-on-discrete-s.tldr: Discrete Flow Models use continuous-time Markov chains to enable joint discrete and continuous generation, demonstrated in protein co-design.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks benefit from information that helps distinguish nodes by their positions and structural roles. Positional and structural encodings provide this information, but choosing encodings that work best across all prediction tasks remains unresolved. The Graph Positional and Structural Encoder, or GPSE, learns representations intended to augment graph neural networks with this information.

GPSE learns a common latent representation for multiple positional and structural encodings. Instead of treating each encoding only as a separately computed input, it captures their information in a learned encoder. The paper emphasizes transfer: an encoder trained on one graph dataset can be used effectively on datasets with substantially different distributions and modalities.

Across a broad benchmark collection, models enhanced with GPSE significantly outperform models using explicitly computed encodings in some cases and at least match them in others. These results support the potential for pretrained graph encoders that supply reusable structural information. The authors also release their framework and pretrained models and report integration into PyG, making the learned representations available for downstream graph prediction applications.
icml-2024-graph-positional-and-structura.tldr: GPSE learns transferable graph position and structure representations that match or improve on explicit encodings across tested benchmarks.

paragraphs: A large neural network can fit every training label while having many more parameters than the data seem to require. This paper studies why even a randomly sampled network can generalize when sampling is conditioned on perfectly classifying the training set. The question separates the effect of the parameter distribution from the usual role of gradient-based training.

The authors prove typical generalization under a specific condition: there exists a narrow teacher network that agrees with the labels. Their explanation is that a flat distribution over parameters does not produce a flat distribution over functions. Redundancy in neural network representations creates a preference for simpler functions that require fewer relevant parameters.

As a result, the sample complexity is approximately proportional to the teacher's complexity, roughly its number of nonredundant parameters, rather than the larger student's complexity. This provides a theoretical explanation for why parameter count alone can be misleading in this setting. The result concerns typical interpolating samples under the narrow-teacher condition; it does not claim that every randomly chosen network generalizes.
icml-2024-how-uniform-random-weights-ind.tldr: Under a narrow-teacher condition, random interpolating networks typically generalize because flat parameter priors favor simpler functions.

paragraphs: Preference optimization trains language models to produce outputs people favor. This paper connects two methods that initially appear different: Identity Policy Optimisation, or IPO, is an offline method, while Nash Mirror Descent, or Nash-MD, operates online using a preference model. The connection emerges when IPO is placed in a particular online setting.

In that setting, both candidate generations come from the current policy and receive annotations from a trained preference model. The authors prove that optimizing IPO on this stream is equivalent to seeking the preference model's Nash equilibrium through self-play. The equivalence therefore depends on how examples are generated and labeled; it is not an unconditional identity between offline and online training.

Building on this result, the paper introduces IPO-MD. It samples from a mixture of the current policy and a reference policy, adopting the regularized sampling idea from Nash-MD. The authors compare online IPO and IPO-MD with online versions of DPO and SLiC on summarization. The stated contribution is the theoretical connection and the resulting algorithm, with an empirical comparison on that task.
icml-2024-human-alignment-of-large-langu.tldr: The paper proves an online IPO–Nash-MD equivalence under specified sampling conditions and introduces the mixture-policy algorithm IPO-MD.

paragraphs: This paper examines how gradient descent trains an associative memory module that stores outer products of token embeddings. To make the learning dynamics tractable, the authors translate the problem into a system of interacting particles. The interactions depend on the data distribution and on correlations among embeddings, connecting the mathematical model to properties of the stored tokens.

Theory and experiments show logarithmic growth of classification margins in overparameterized regimes. They also reveal temporary oscillations caused by unequal token frequencies and interference between correlated embeddings. Larger step sizes make these oscillations more pronounced and can create benign loss spikes, even while speeding the dynamics and improving asymptotic convergence.

The findings distinguish transient instability from long-run learning behavior: a spike in loss can occur within a process that ultimately converges faster. The paper also finds that underparameterized regimes produce suboptimal memorization schemes. Finally, the authors assess their findings on small Transformer models, checking how insights from the isolated memory module relate to behavior in those models.
icml-2024-learning-associative-memories-.tldr: A particle-system analysis links associative-memory learning dynamics to token imbalance, embedding interference, and step-size-dependent loss spikes.

paragraphs: Imitation learning is most straightforward when demonstrations show high-quality behavior. When the available examples are imperfect, copying them can restrict the quality of the learned policy. PAIL adds a limited amount of expert preference feedback to help the learner distinguish better behavior and improve beyond the demonstrations it initially receives.

The algorithm learns a preference reward from expert judgments about imperfect demonstrations. It uses this reward in two ways: to reweight the original demonstrations toward higher quality, and to select newly explored trajectories with high cumulative reward. Those selected trajectories are added to the demonstration data, creating a training set whose quality improves over time.

This connects preference learning to both data selection and continued exploration. The learner is guided by the original examples, but its training data can grow to include better behavior discovered during learning. Experiments on a synthetic task and two locomotion benchmarks show performance exceeding the initial demonstrations. The abstract reports a 73.2% improvement over baselines, supporting the usefulness of limited preference feedback in the evaluated imperfect-demonstration settings.
icml-2024-limited-preference-aided-imita.tldr: PAIL uses limited expert preferences to reweight demonstrations and add better explored trajectories, enabling learning beyond imperfect examples.

paragraphs: Long contexts increase the memory needed to store a language model's attention keys and values. LoCoCo keeps this KV cache at a fixed size by learning how to combine older information with incoming tokens. Its goal is to preserve useful context through adaptive fusion, rather than deciding which stored pairs to discard using heuristics.

The method inserts one-dimensional convolutional kernels that compute mixing weights for each cache slot. These weights determine how information is integrated as new tokens arrive. The paper describes the approach as compatible with existing LLM frameworks, requiring minimal tuning overhead and supporting both inference and fine-tuning.

In inference experiments, LoCoCo compresses up to 3,482 tokens into a cache of size 128 while retaining performance comparable to processing the full sequence. It reports accuracy gains of up to 0.2791 over baselines with the same cache size. During post-training tuning, it extends context length from 4K to 32K with a fixed cache of 512, achieving performance similar to full-sequence fine-tuning. These are demonstrated compression outcomes in the reported experiments.
icml-2024-lococo-dropping-in-convolution.tldr: LoCoCo learns convolutional mixing weights to compress long contexts into a fixed-size KV cache during inference and fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Autoregressive language models generate tokens sequentially, repeatedly moving model parameters into accelerator cache. Medusa reduces the number of these decoding steps by adding heads that predict several upcoming tokens in parallel. A tree-based attention mechanism lets the model verify multiple candidate continuations together, avoiding the need to maintain a separate draft model.

The paper offers two training options. Medusa-1 trains the added heads while keeping the backbone frozen and supports lossless inference acceleration. Medusa-2 trains the heads and backbone together for more accurate predictions and higher speed, using a specialized recipe to preserve model capabilities. These options provide different ways to adapt the existing model.

Additional extensions include self-distillation when training data are unavailable and an acceptance scheme designed to accept more proposed tokens while maintaining generation quality. Across models of different sizes and training procedures, Medusa-1 achieves speedups above 2.2 times without compromising generation quality. Medusa-2 reaches 2.3–2.8 times speedup. The reported benefit comes from doing more useful generation work within each decoding step.
icml-2024-medusa-simple-llm-inference-ac.tldr: Medusa accelerates LLM generation by proposing multiple future tokens with added decoding heads and verifying candidate continuations together.

paragraphs: Imitation learning from observations must learn from expert behavior without seeing which actions the expert took. MAAD addresses this missing information using an inverse dynamics model. Given two successive expert states, this model infers a distribution over plausible actions that could explain the transition, providing an approximate action signal.

The learner is trained with a surrogate reward, which can come from adversarial games, trajectory matching, or optimal transport criteria. MAAD adds a regularizer that aligns the learner's policy with the inferred action distribution. The inferred distribution therefore complements the reward rather than serving as the only source of learning guidance.

The paper evaluates this on-policy algorithm in MuJoCo environments from OpenAI Gym and the DeepMind Control Suite. It reports greater stability and substantially improved sample efficiency relative to current state-of-the-art on-policy methods, requiring fewer environment interactions to reach expert performance. In many of the reported comparisons, MAAD alone reaches that level. The findings support using plausible action distributions to make observation-only imitation more effective in the tested environments.
icml-2024-mimicking-better-by-matching-t.tldr: MAAD improves observation-only imitation by aligning the learner's policy with action distributions inferred from expert state transitions.

paragraphs: Feature attribution methods aim to identify which parts of an input most influence a model's decision. Gradients can provide useful attribution signals, but computing them requires access to model internals. That access may be unavailable, including for safety-related reasons. GEEX is designed for the more restricted setting where an explainer can only submit queries and observe model outputs.

The method estimates gradients to produce gradient-like explanations through this query interface. This makes the access requirement central to the contribution: the explainer seeks information similar to that used by gradient-based methods without directly reading the model's internal derivatives. The authors also rigorously prove a set of fundamental attribution properties for the approach.

Experiments focus on image data and compare GEEX with both black-box methods and methods that have full model access. The paper reports superior results against state-of-the-art black-box alternatives and competitive performance against full-access methods. Together, the formal properties and image experiments support the usefulness of gradient estimation for explanations, without establishing universal equivalence to every white-box method.
icml-2024-on-gradient-like-explanation-u.tldr: GEEX produces gradient-like feature explanations using only model queries, with proven attribution properties and competitive image results.

paragraphs: Stochastic neural architectures can support uncertainty quantification, robustness, and memory efficiency, but their computation can be costly. This paper introduces a family of infinitely deep Bayesian neural networks that uses partial stochasticity. The design aims to retain benefits associated with fully stochastic models while reducing the computational burden during both training and inference.

The authors develop several architectural configurations, including different ways of partitioning weights. This makes partial stochasticity a flexible design choice within the infinite-depth framework. They also prove that the family consists of universal conditional distribution approximators, providing a mathematical expressivity guarantee about the conditional distributions these models can approximate.

Empirical evaluations across multiple tasks show better downstream performance and uncertainty quantification than the compared counterparts, alongside significantly greater efficiency. These results connect the architecture's computational motivation with measured predictive behavior. The approximation theorem and the experiments address complementary questions: the theorem establishes representational capacity for the model family, while the evaluations show practical benefits for the particular tasks and configurations tested.
icml-2024-partially-stochastic-infinitel.tldr: Partially stochastic infinite-depth Bayesian networks combine universal conditional distribution approximation with improved efficiency and uncertainty estimates in experiments.

paragraphs: Visual reprogramming adapts a pretrained model by adding a learned pattern to input images, avoiding the need to tune many internal model parameters. A mask usually specifies where that pattern appears, and existing approaches often share the same predefined mask across images. This paper shows that such sharing can limit generalization and increase approximation error.

The proposed sample-specific multi-channel mask framework, SMM, makes the mask depend on the individual image. A lightweight convolutional network and patch-wise interpolation generate a separate three-channel mask for each sample. The key change is therefore in how the prompt is placed across the input, adding adaptation at the sample level.

The authors theoretically show reduced target-task approximation error compared with existing state-of-the-art visual reprogramming methods. They also demonstrate empirical performance gains with both ResNet and Vision Transformer backbones. These findings support input-dependent masks as a way to improve the use of pretrained knowledge through visual prompting, while keeping the adaptation focused on the input pattern and its placement.
icml-2024-sample-specific-masks-for-visu.tldr: SMM improves visual reprogramming by generating a separate three-channel prompt mask for each input image.

paragraphs: Associative memory can recover a stored pattern or connect it to other related patterns. Correlated Dense Associative Memory, or CDAM, brings these two behaviors into one framework for continuous-valued memories. An arbitrary graph specifies semantic relationships between patterns, giving the memory system an explicit structure for moving among related content.

Theoretical and numerical analysis identifies four dynamical modes: recall of a pattern itself, narrow association with related patterns, wider association, and a neutral quiet state. The model uses anti-Hebbian learning rules, inspired by inhibitory modulation studies, to control the range of association. This allows the dynamics to reflect different scales of relationships among memories.

The paper uses these mechanisms to extract graph community structure at multiple scales and stabilize recall of temporal sequences. Demonstrations include real-world data, image retrieval, replication of a classical neuroscience experiment, and simulation of arbitrary finite automata. Together, these applications show how graph-linked memories can support both retrieval and structured sequences of activity within the same proposed model.
icml-2024-semantically-correlated-memori.tldr: CDAM uses graph-linked memories and controlled association dynamics to support retrieval, community representations, and temporal sequence recall.

paragraphs: Controlling generated text becomes expensive when a system must handle changing or multiple target subjects. Existing decoding-based methods can require new training when the control target changes, and simultaneous controls can add substantial cost. SF-Gen addresses this by separating reusable information about language generation from the rewards associated with particular control goals.

The paper first expresses existing approaches as reinforcement learning problems. In this view, an action-value function estimates the likelihood that generated text will exhibit a desired attribute. SF-Gen then uses successor features to decouple the language model's dynamics from task-specific rewards, making the control framework less tightly tied to an individual target.

The authors report memory and computational efficiency during both training and decoding, especially with multiple subjects. Across controllable generation experiments, the method produces text comparable to state-of-the-art approaches in control and language quality, while outperforming baselines. The contribution combines a reusable representation for control with empirical evidence that improved efficiency can coexist with strong generated-text quality in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2024-successor-features-for-efficie.tldr: SF-Gen separates language-generation dynamics from control rewards using successor features, improving efficiency for multiple target subjects.

paragraphs: A neural network can be viewed as a sequence of composed mappings, with each mapping playing a role similar to a word in a sentence. However, freely varying the weights of linear mappings would require infinitely many such words. This paper asks whether a finite vocabulary of mappings can still provide universal approximation.

The authors constructively prove that a vocabulary containing O(d²) mappings from d-dimensional space to itself is sufficient. For any continuous target mapping, any compact domain, and any positive error tolerance, some finite sequence of vocabulary elements composes into an approximation within that tolerance. The vocabulary is finite, while the sequence can vary with the approximation problem.

The result shows that rich approximation power can come from composing a fixed collection of operations. Its guarantee is specifically about continuous mappings on compact domains and permits the composition length to vary. The paper uses this perspective to motivate a compositional model for regular languages, connecting function approximation with the idea of constructing expressive sequences from a limited vocabulary.
icml-2024-vocabulary-for-universal-appro.tldr: A finite vocabulary of O(d²) mappings can approximate any continuous d-dimensional mapping on a compact domain through suitable compositions.

paragraphs: If future models perform tasks that humans cannot reliably judge, alignment will have to work with weaker supervision. This paper studies an analogy: whether a weak model can supervise a stronger pretrained model and bring out capabilities beyond its own. The experiments cover natural language processing, chess, and reward modeling using models in the GPT-4 family.

Simply fine-tuning stronger models on weak-model labels consistently produces models that outperform their supervisors. The authors call this weak-to-strong generalization. However, this naive procedure recovers substantially less than the stronger models' full capabilities, suggesting that extending existing supervision-based alignment techniques to superhuman systems may require additional work.

Simple changes can often improve the result. With a GPT-2-level supervisor and an auxiliary confidence loss, fine-tuning GPT-4 recovers close to GPT-3.5-level performance on NLP tasks. The finding supports the possibility of eliciting knowledge that the supervisor cannot fully express. It also establishes an empirical setting for studying weak supervision today, without treating success in this model-to-model analogy as a completed solution to superhuman alignment.
icml-2024-weak-to-strong-generalization-.tldr: Strong pretrained models can outperform weak supervisors after fine-tuning, but recovering their full capabilities requires more than naive weak-label training.
